paras: The Boaz hanging ordeal and expulsion took place on January 17, 1903, when about a dozen men hanged two Black men from trees in the woods near Boaz, Marshall County, Alabama, after they were accused of stealing meat from a local merchant. The men were cut down alive, confessed, and were driven out of town, and the dispatch reported that the people of Boaz would not tolerate Black residents. The story ran as a short wire item in white papers from Alabama to South Dakota; no Black-press coverage was found.

According to a Gadsden special, the two men were accused of stealing "a quantity of meat" from "a leading merchant of Boaz" and denied the theft. None of the accounts names the men, the merchant or anyone involved, and none mentions an arrest or any officer.

After the denial, the men were taken into the woods, nooses were placed around their necks, and the ropes were thrown over trees. They were then "pulled up by a dozen men" and left hanging until, in the dispatch's words, "life was nearly extinct." When they were almost dead they were cut down, and once able to talk they confessed to the theft.

The Montgomery Advertiser's version said instead that the men, once lowered, told where the meat was hidden and that it was recovered. Both men were then driven out of town, or in the Advertiser's phrase "made to leave."

The reports closed with the statement that the people of Boaz had announced they would not tolerate "negro citizens." No report of arrests, an investigation or any official response appears in the coverage.

The story first appeared on January 18 as a Gadsden special, relayed through Chattanooga, in the Louisville Courier-Journal, the Houston Daily Post and the Indianapolis Journal, while the Montgomery Advertiser printed its own Gadsden special the same day. Reprints followed in the Rock Island Argus on January 19, the Americus Times-Recorder on January 20 and the Turner County Herald of Hurley, South Dakota, on January 22.

Most papers called the men "negro thieves" and treated the theft as settled, with headlines such as "Negro Thieves Hanged to Trees" in Louisville and "Negro Thieves Swung by Mob" in Americus. The Advertiser headlined it "Thieves Are Strung Up" and wrote that the men "soon were swinging into eternity," though its own text had them lowered alive. The Indianapolis Journal alone framed the episode as abuse, under the headline "Two Negroes Tortured," and the South Dakota item described the men as "tried by the ordeal of hanging" and confessing "to save their lives." No editorial comment on the episode appears in the coverage, and no account of it was found in the Black press.

reader.title: Boaz hanging ordeal and expulsion
bases: A dozen men hanged two accused Black men from trees until nearly dead to force a confession, cut them down alive, and drove them out of town (A1, A3, A6); no one was killed.

A group of about a dozen men, acting without legal authority on an accusation of meat theft, hanged the two men, but both were cut down alive (A1, A3, A4), so no one was killed and the standard definition is not met; it was a non-fatal hanging ordeal followed by expulsion.

All accounts descend from Gadsden specials filed the same day (A1, A2, A3) and reprinted elsewhere (A4-A7); the Montgomery Advertiser's version (A2) differs in wording but not in substance, and no independent local or Black-press report was found.

framing.detail: The Alabama paper headlined 'Thieves Are Strung Up', treated the theft as established and closed with the flat statement that Boaz 'will not tolerate negro citizens'.
Louisville, Houston and Americus ran the wire text calling the men 'negro thieves', under headlines such as 'Negro Thieves Hanged to Trees' and 'Negro Thieves Swung by Mob'.
The Indianapolis Journal ran the same text but headlined it 'Two Negroes Tortured', presenting the hanging as coercion to force a confession.

versions.value: Cut down when almost dead; confessed to the theft once able to talk

conflicts.note: Compatible versions; only the Montgomery Advertiser reports recovery of the meat. Its phrase 'swinging into eternity' is contradicted within the same article by the men being lowered alive.
The Courier-Journal headline names Gadsden, the dateline city; its own text and every other account say the men were driven from Boaz.
